column12: message

Punishment is a more immediate and impactful method than positive reinforcement, particularly for certain behaviors. For instance, individuals who drive under the influence of alcohol may face imprisonment. Such punishments make people aware of what behaviors are harmful and unacceptable, and they are more likely to modify their behavior accordingly. In contrast, positive reinforcement may take longer to produce results. If individuals do not change their behavior, it can lead to tragic consequences, such as the loss of innocent lives in drunk driving accidents. The threat of imprisonment or other penalties is intended to discourage people from committing crimes in the first place. Dr. Driscoll emphasized that in all instances, the individual administering punishment for some misbehavior does so with the expectation that the behavior will stop and not be repeated. (Chapter 2, page 42) So, I support punishment is more effective than positive reinforcement as a method for changing behavior.

I agree, going to jail is a strong enough consequence to keep some from driving under the influence but I wonder if the positive outcomes to not driving under the influence are more impactful. For example, lower insurance rates are a reward for not participating in risky behaviors that could lead to a DUI. I also like feeling confident, like I am in control and safely driving. When I do those things I feel good about myself and adds to my self esteem. Taking it one step further, when my children see me making good choices it rubs off on them, who are always watching. They will be safe and empowered to drive safely and that is a positive outcome that keeps me from driving under the influence as well.

I understand your point, as the textbook we read this week said, positive reinforcement can strengthen an operant behavior. Setting positive examples for children and teaching them to make good choices can have long-term benefits for their safety and well-being.

However, it is important to remember that penalties can also act as a deterrent to those who may consider drinking and driving (for adults). While positive reinforcement may be effective for some people, others may need the stimulus of punishment to avoid engaging in risky behaviors. We have no way to divide the crowd in advance, and punishment has a deterrent effect on more people, and the consequences of unacceptable behavior will be considered. From this, it can be seen that the threat of punishment is a more effective method to promote safe driving than positive reinforcement.

Punishment in many incidents does do a better job of controlling the outcome than positive reinforcement. I like your example of jail or imprisonment for those who chose to drive while intoxicated. Jail is an immediate consequence that at least scares the majority of people away from committing crimes. A smaller scale of this type of punishment that I have found effective with some students is a timeout or taking away a privileged item. If a freedom is taken away, and that freedom is highly desired, people will likely do whatever they can/will to keep that freedom.

I would like to also consider the way others can use punishment as a way to manipulate a system to their benefit. Sometimes others will create false scenarios that to cause others to get into trouble when they maybe they actually haven't done anything wrong. This can happen easily in a classroom where a teacher may be overwhelmed or unaware with exactly what is happening in their surroundings. This is an uncommon scenario but happens enough and when punishment is consistent it can be pointed in the wrong direction.

I don't agree with the example given. There are a lot of people who get imprisoned who are repeat offenders. So the punishment of being put in prison is not enough for them to change their behavior. However, there are less likely to be repeat offenders when there is prison reform and support for people who have addictions such as alcoholism which increases their chances of driving drunk. That's why I think positive reinforcement is a better solution than punishment.

While punishment has its place and can be effective for making quick changes in behavior, it can also lead to some unhealthy consequences. It is hard to learn when you are afraid or under stress, when you are managing the nervous system and new information. Positive reinforcement plays an important role in building up a learner's self esteem, putting the nerves at ease and supporting self awareness. The old adage is, "you get more flies with honey" and it is a great example of using a positive stimulus to attract a positive result (we can pretend flies are a positive output).

I agree with your idea that positive reinforcement plays an important role in building a learner's self-esteem, relaxing nerves, and supporting self-awareness. While positive reinforcement may take longer to see results in behavior, there are situations where we need to quickly address and stop unwanted behavior. What are some effective strategies that we can implement in those scenarios? For example, if a child is about to injure herself by picking up a hot iron, a fast slap on the wrist of a loud "NO!" may be the most effective way to gain her attention and stop her in the act. (Driscoll, p.42)

I agree with 85767's point and would also like to add the phenomena of "learned helplessness" in which an individual receives constant punishment or negative comments about a certain behavior that eventually leads them to give up on attempting to change or improve their efforts. This is a consequence of using punishment to change a student's behavior, when positive reinforcement can have more lasting and uplifting effects on a student's behavior and performance.

I agree with 59488's point. In certain situation's it may be more important to quickly discourage behavior. Also, when positive reinforcement occurs just once, it is likely that it will not teach a new behavior and partial reinforcement is more effective once a behavior has already been somewhat established.

Learned helplessness is definitely an issue that can arise from the constant use of punishment, but with the constant use of positive reinforcements can create attention-seeking behaviors in students. Anytime a student whines and is given the desired attention, it can show them that whining = attention and can create that attention-seeking behavior. Both require a delicate balance of use to be effective with students to keep them safe as well as prevent negative behaviors from forming.

I agree that it can cause unhealthy consequences. I feel like punishment can have really negative effects on children's mental health and cause kids to be very anxious. Especially when children are getting punished for an unjustified reason. I always feel like positive reinforcement really boosted my confidence. Especially in school environments, when teachers focused on positive reinforcement I felt very safe in their classrooms. I love that saying, "you get more flies with honey" I have never heard that before!

THORNDIKE & SKINNER 

Thorndike’s Law of Effect modified the classic principal of associated that “would have far-reaching implications for behaviorism” (Driscoll). Through his experiments, he found that an animal “learned to associate a sensation and an impulse when its action had a satisfying consequence” (Driscoll). In admitting a satisfying consequence (positive reinforcement) to an action, the animal was able to learn the behavior and successively repeat it, showing is success. Similarly, B.F. Skinner’s concept of reinforcement derived from Thorndike’s Law of Effect, explaining that “behavior is more likely to occur again if it is rewarded, or reinforced,” again, supporting the notion of positive reinforcement. Skinner’s concept of Shaping also involves positive reinforcement, “in that a reinforcer is contingent upon desired behavior” (Driscoll). These theories serve as the building blocks of behaviorism, and corroborate the practice of positive reinforcement as the most effective form of changing behavior. In no ways did these initial experiments support punishment as the act of changing behavior, and Skinner himself was opposed to punishment because of its negative effects posed on the individual, such as aggression and emotional trauma.

In fact, punishment has many adverse effects that do more harm than good in attempting to change behavior in individuals. Long history of punishment “may cause physical or psychological harm,” and in situations of inescapable stimuli, individuals may develop the concept of learned helplessness, the “passive acceptance of events seemingly beyond one’s control” causing individuals to essentially give up or stop trying (Driscoll). It has also been found that not only does punishment negatively impact an individual’s being, its effectiveness “tends to be short-lived,” in that the behavior may continue if the stimuli inducing the punishment is not present to do so (Driscoll).

I agree with 37229's stance and would like to also add another layer to the negatives of punishment in behaviorism. According to the Driscoll text, "punishment can serve as a model for aggression. In a series of studies examining aggressive behavior in children, Bandura, Ross, and Ross (1961, 1963) demonstrated that those who observed others being aggressive were more likely to be aggressive themselves This is further supported by evidence from studies of abusive families; by and large, parents who are abusive were themselves abused as children (Steinmetz, 1977; Stiauss, Gelles, & Stein·metz, 1980)." pg. 41. While not all punishment may be aggressive or abusive, the outcome of punishing a student for poor behavior or performance can create an unhealthy power dynamic that creates an ecosystem for anger to grow. Encouraging a student with positive reinforcement, boundaries and helpful feedback creates a healthy learning environment where the learners feel supported.

While positive reinforcement may be effective for maintaining behavior or emphasizing positive behavior, in a classroom setting if an unwanted behavior is repeatedly occurring, positive reinforcement may no longer be effective, as a child may continue to think that their behavior is permitted/allowable unless (behavior unrelated to performance).

Starting students off with clear expectations surrounding how certain classroom activities will be preformed is one way to mitigate poor behaviors from students. For example, it is unfair to assume that all children know how to line up to go to lunch. Clear expectations given with consistency and positive reinforcement will encourage all students to move and transition between tasks in supportive way. I would even go as far to say that when students are misbehaving in this environment it is a tell that more support and care need to be brought in. Maybe they had a rough morning at home and need an extra check in from their teacher.

While punishment can have negative effects, it is still a necessary tool for behavior change. Punishment can cause physical or psychological harm, but this is not always the case. It is important to use appropriate forms of punishment and to avoid excessive punishment. For example, corporal punishment is generally considered to be harmful, but other forms of punishment, such as time-outs or loss of privileges, can be effective without causing harm.
In some cases, punishment can lead to learned helplessness, but, learned helplessness is more likely to occur when punishment is excessive or when individuals are punished for things that are beyond their control.

As a high school teacher in a district that is going through a massive overhaul to its code of conduct, I can say that behavior has been a push to remove extreme punishments like ISS and OSS. The loss of instructional time had become pretty severe. And there has been a lot of consternation from many teachers that support the position of punishment as being effective. But the data has not borne out that view. There has been growth at schools where the loss of instructional time has decreased. While that could be correlation and not causation, it is at least worth exploring further.

A PERSONAL EXPERIENCE REGARDING POSITIVE REINFORCEMENT

In my personal experience, there has been a situation in which positive reinforcement proved to be more successful in changing a behavior than punishment. In my 4 years at NC State, I was an active member of the sorority, Delta Zeta. As a requirement, every member had to attend the chapter meetings every Sunday night. The punishment for not attending chapter was a fine, the amount depending on if the meeting was formal or informal. Low attendance at chapter had always been a problem in the sorority, and the threatening of fining individuals created a very negative connotation around the concept of our meetings and the attitude of the sorority has a whole. In attempting to combat this issue, one of our new presidents decided to bring dessert every Sunday night to chapter, and all members who attended chapter were allowed the treat. This drastically increased the number of individuals who attended the meetings, and created a positive environment as women were allowed to eat the treats during the meeting. This was a simple way in enticing members to attend the meetings and create a more enjoyable environment that people actually wanted to come to. This is just one example of how positive reinforcement proved to be more effective than punishment.

Hi 37229! I think the using desserts as a reinforcer is a very creative take. I have experience in similar situations as the chapter president of Kappa Delta where we use fines as a punishment for missing rounds of recruitment. This is a situation where there is no kind of positive reinforcement that can be added to support the target behavior (sisters showing up for rounds) , so fining is the better method.

I completely agree with you. I have personally always responded better to positive reinforcement. In my classroom in first grade, my teacher would always hand out prizes and rewards such as Skittles when we answered questions or behaved well in her class. It made learning fun and increased the amount that her students were participating. This worked a lot better than some of my teachers who were punishing us by making us walk laps at recess or handing out silent lunch. I feel like we just ended up resenting our teacher and it caused more bad behavior.

Punishment is applying unpleasant stimulus or removing pleasant stimulus as a deterrent to behavior that is not desired, whereas positive reinforcement is reward of a desired behavior. 

Behavior is more likely to reoccur if it has been rewarded or reinforced. Similarly, a response is less likely to occur again if it has been aversive (Driscoll, p. 35). Punishment is more effective than positive reinforcement because punishment can be immediate and more demotivating. It can be applied immediately after unwanted behavior which makes it more likely that an individual will learn that the behavior is associated with a negative consequence. In contrast, positive reinforcement may not be applied immediately after the behavior which can make it less effective. The negative consequences of punishment can reduce one’s motivation to engage in unwanted behavior.

I agree with the idea of 8036's post. When trying to discourage behavior, punishment is more effective compared to positive reinforcement which will encourage the behavior and also may take a longer time to impact behavior.

I agree, 8036. It is important to acknowledge that individuals may not always realize when their behavior is inappropriate. Nevertheless, the strategic use of punishment can prove to be a powerful method in curbing such undesirable actions.

I see your point in that punishment is more immediate in its timing of response to a behavior, but according to Driscoll, it's "effectiveness tends to be short-lived," meaning that the behavior may immediately stop in the moment, but will continue on throughout time when the punishment/punisher doesn't seem to be present. This supports the notion that positive reinforcement tends to have more lasting effects on punishment on changing a behavior.

Based on personal personal experience with students and my child, positive reinforcement encouraged them to behave appropriately for a reward and when none was offered the negative behaviors resurfaced. On the other hand, punishment such as time out allowed my child to associate throwing toys with a negative consequence and the behavior was reduced and eventually stopped. With students, punishment such as switching lunch tables away from their friends allowed them to associate talking back to the cafeteria assistants to that negative consequence, thereby curtailing the behavior.

Punishment can be more effective than positive reinforcement to decrease negative/unwanted behavior. According to our textbook for this course, punishment is the presentation of an aversive stimulus contingent upon a response that reduces the rate of that response (Driscoll, 2005). While positive reinforcement can be useful for strengthening/reinforcing a behavior, punishment is more effective for decreasing unwanted behavior.

Positive reinforcement has its strengths in decreasing unwanted behavior as well, by providing a more uplifting and encouraging attitude to changing a behavior, avoiding the adverse effects that punishment can have on an individual's mental and physical health, especially when administered to developing students.

37229, I am not sure I have ever seen someone fail because of someone trying to uplift and encourage them. However, I have seen many students give up trying to do the right thing because the punishment was always going to happen. Learned helplessness is all over the students I teach. It is the direct result of punishments meted out with no thought given to the many consequences it could have had. A temporary decrease in some unwanted behavior was the window dressing to impacting the student's growth as a student and a person.

Punishment is more effective than positive reinforcement when used/applied immediately to stop behavior. For example, consider the example of a child who is playing around a stove. A parent may grab the child’s hand, raise their voice to tell them to move from the stove or utilize some other form of punishment to quickly make it known that it is not safe/behavior that the child should be engaging in. In this case, punishment is likely more efficient for changing behavior compared to positive reinforcement where a parent would have to encourage playing in a different environment or wait till the child moves away from the stove to reinforce that behavior.

Yes, punishment can be an effective way to communicate what behaviors are acceptable or not in certain situations. For example, in some cultural traditions, yelling is not tolerated. If a kid is yelling without any emergency, the punishment will be served for his behavior, and the kid will be aware that his yelling behaviors are not acceptable at all. The consequence of punishment will be more effective for this given situation.

I agree- additionally, punishment is often more immediate and easier than a positive reinforcement and more suitable for a situation like the one you mentioned above that requires quick action. The promise of a positive reinforcer yet to come may not be as impactful

While punishment can lead to long term negative consequences, particularly if physical, not all punishment falls under this form. For example, negative punishment, which is when a stimulus is removed in order to decrease a behavior. Examples of negative punishment include not allowing an individual to use a toy/device, not getting a reward token, etc. are forms of negative punishment which can be used to discourage a particular behavior, and then the stimulus can be returned.

Hi 63749! I agree- I mostly use negative punishment at my work where I nanny a 4 year old. The most effective tools when trying to correct behavior is threatening (and sometimes following through) with temporarily taking away a favorite toy, or saying she can't have a cookie after dinner. The threat of this alone is usually very effective in stopping whatever behavior needs to be stopped.

Hi 63749! I agree with your stance on punishment over positive reinforcement. Many times in my experience, I have seen punishment be a more effective method of student/child management than positive reinforcement. One of my main reasons for punishments is for the child's safety. Many of the children I have looked after or babysat are 2-6 years old, they're still learning and testing all of the boundaries they can. When it comes to their safety, I have found they learn more with punishments like a timeout.

Here is my personal experience with a situation where punishment proves to be the more effective method- 

I nanny a 4 year old who, like most kids her age, just doesn't want to leave the playground, go have rest time etc. every now and then. Since I am solely responsible for her during the time I watch her, I have to help her learn that this is not good behavior in the most gentile and supportive way I can. I have watched her since she was 2, and adding a positive reinforcer like offering a treat or special priviledge does not work when she is being defiant. The most effective solution in this situation is for me to introduce a punishment like sitting in time out or not being able to watch cartoons.

As a former nanny/babysitter, I also found that punishment would work more effectively in these situations than rewards. While removing the child from the playground may seem like a punishment to the child at the time, by bringing in a "bigger" punishment to the situation the child will be more inclined to comply with what is needed of them. At times the reward can also turn into a safety issue if not careful.

60685 and 40519, I would like to add that punishment should also be used in conjunction with other behavior change strategies. In addition, it should also fit the behavior. The examples you stated sounded fitting based on your role, relationship with the child and the information you gained from implementing the consequence for the behavior.

In many cases, punishment is a more effective method of changing a person's behavior. In larger classrooms where teachers may be handling more than one student, many teachers have found that punishment based on behaviorism provides a better method of classroom management (Driscoll, p. 60). In grade school, we had a tally chart or stick chart for each one of our classes. Everyone started with a stick or a pin in the green at the beginning of the day. If we misbehaved during class, the stick would be moved to yellow as a warning and then to red which had a set punishment for each variation of incidents. Having students see where they stood on the behavior chart helped them self-manage their behavior throughout the class. This method took the strain off of the teacher in the majority of minor misbehaviors.

Hi 40519! You just unlocked a memory when you mentioned that stick charts from elementary school. This is such a good representation of punishment being effectively used in a classroom setting as I can still remember how impactful having to move a stick was 15 years later! This example shows punishment being used as a quick way for teachers to correct behaviors without disrupting the whole class.

I agree with you both. I have had similar experiences which I recount with siblings and friends. The behaviors that had punishment associated with them were ones I quickly learned to correct. I remember those even now, so many years later. This is true for both home and school.

I do agree, at first, that punishment can be a quick way to control a larger group. However, as discussed by Driscoll, some students might be acting out to receive the "punishment." This punishment system only works when the punishment is somethings the students, as a collective, do not want. Self-managing behavior is something that adults can't do all the time, so I can't believe that students in grade school can achieve it a high enough level to be effective.

I believe that punishment can be very anxiety-inducing to children. I personally would not want to use punishment in a classroom if I was a teacher because I do not know what children's home lives are all the time. Some children might fear their parents because of how they punish them, and I would not want them to associate negative feelings with my classroom. I think it would especially bad to use punishment on children who are people pleasers because it would cause them a lot of stress to get in trouble.

In solidarity to your opposition (I am tried of saying I agree), punishments only work if they decrease in the specific undesired responses. Punishments seem to be universal, i.e. each "crime" has the same punishment. The same punishment doesn't work for every person/kid/student.

One way that I have particularly seen positive reinforcement work well is at my job at a public library. We hand out stickers to children who are checking out books. The kids get really excited about getting the stickers and it makes them want to come back to the library and read more. We also give out prizes when you do certain reading activities and complete the list of activities. This positive reinforcement encourages children to read and gives them positive associations with the library.

I would like to try and reframe this statement.

Punishment seems to be considered the positive reinforcement of adding an aversive stimulus after the unwanted behavior. But it could also be the negative reinforcement of removing a wanted stimulus. So I assuming we are directly talking about positive reinforcement of adding a desired stimulus after desired behavior.  I will bluntly say that you get more flies with honey than with vinegar.

As we've been learning thus far, Behaviorism, as a psychological theory, emphasizes the importance of consequences in shaping behavior. Punishment and positive reinforcement are both forms of consequences, but punishment specifically focuses on discouraging undesirable behavior through negative consequences. This can lead to quicker behavior modification and explicit expectations or standards. So when we think about the statement, "punishment is more effective than positive reinforcement as a method for changing behavior," within the foundational domain of behaviorism as mentioned above, then we can understand that immediate and consistent consequences via punishment are crucial effective behavior modification. Such immediate consequences creates a clear association between the undesirable behavior and the consequence. This can thus facilitate faster, positive learning outcomes and behavioral changes compared to the typical delayed consequences seen via positive reinforcement. Punishment also allows for a broader application, whereas positive reinforcement usually works only within a singe context situation; which, may also prompt confusion in other future, similar scenarios or instances of negative behavior. Punishment, instead, can lead to a generalization of negative consequences (or a fear so to speak of negative consequences) that undesirable behavior across contrasting scenarios may be suppressed to avoid any similar repercussions. This not only results in a broader change in overall behavior compared to positive reinforcement, but can further expedite the extinction of most if not all undesirable behavior; especially, if clear expectations of acceptable behavior moving forward are conveyed through the punishment.

Hi 64758!

I thought you had solid arguments in support, but I want to examine this statement. “This not only results in a broader change in overall behavior compared to positive reinforcement, but can further expedite the extinction of most if not all undesirable behavior; especially, if clear expectations of acceptable behavior moving forward are conveyed through the punishment.”

What could be clearer than rewarding someone for doing a desired behavior? An upset learner cannot always hear beyond what is being taken away from them. They do not always even understand what they did wrong. Not all people can use punishment consequences in broader contexts because their motivation isn't always to get it right. A good example for is the student that keeps acting out to get attention.

Hey 64758! Overall, I can see where you are coming from in your argument for this post. However, I do have a question about one statement. "Such immediate consequences creates a clear association between the undesirable behavior and the consequence." I do not believe that this can be true at the same time as punishment creating a lower sense of self worth overtime as suggested by the American Association of Pediatrics. I understand that the immediate consequence may help in the short term, but do you not feel that it may cause negative associations with their decision making skills in the future? Where is the line between hurting and helping their emotional devlopment?

Hi 47520! Thank you for your response and raising a valid concern regarding the potential negative effects of immediate consequences associated with punishment on a child's emotional development. I do think it's essential to consider both sides of this argument in order to have a comprehensive understanding. So while I think it's been shown that immediate consequences, especially in the form of punishment, can create a clear association between undesirable behavior and the consequence, it's definitely crucial to acknowledge the potential impact on a child's emotional well-being and self-esteem. The American Association of Pediatrics rightfully emphasizes the importance of considering a child's emotional development in behavioral interventions. However, I don't think this is such a black and white issue and that it's further essential to note that the effectiveness of punishment in behavior modification largely depends on its appropriateness, fairness, and proportionality to the specific undesirable behavior. A well-structured and just punishment, coupled with clear communication about why the consequence is being administered, can greatly help a child understand the implications of their actions without causing lasting damage to their self-worth; especially, if the undesirable behavior is significantly inappropriate, such as hitting or fighting with other children unprovokedly. Judiciously applied punishment can thus act as a deterrent for undesirable behavior, encouraging the child to make better choices in the future. In this sense, the punishment acts as a learning opportunity for the child, and should they face a similar situation in the future, they will have the active recall of their past experience to make a better, critical decision and modify their behavior accordingly. Immediate consequences, including punishment when done in this way, can yield faster behavior modification, but it should definitely be accompanied by guidance and support to help the child understand and internalize the desired behaviors.

Hi 50400! Thank you for your insightful feedback and for pointing out a crucial aspect of this discussion. It's definitely interesting to explore the effectiveness of positive reinforcement and consider potential challenges in only applying that method or punishment as a method for behavior modification. I think to an extent, if done precisely and consistently, positive reinforcement could provide clear rewards for desired behavior, and for many learners, this approach could be effective and motivating. I definitely recognize how the sense of accomplishment and recognition gained from positive reinforcement can eventually reinforce positive behavior and encourage children to continue engaging in those behaviors. However, I think it's also important to recognize that different children/individuals will respond differently to various forms of reinforcement and consequences. While positive reinforcement may work well for some, I think there are cases where proper punishment will be more effective, especially when combined with clear communication and guidance. In your example of a student seeking attention through negative behavior, it's definitely important to carefully evaluate the underlying motives and tailor an approach accordingly. Punishment when applied appropriately, and proportionately especially being the key here, can serve as a deterrent and help the individual understand the consequences of their actions. This can be a valuable learning experience, reinforcing the understanding of acceptable behavior and encouraging a shift in behavior towards more positive alternatives. I think it's further important to note that punishment can still incorporate elements of clear communication about what was done wrong and what is expected moving forward. This can guide the learner in understanding the specific behaviors that need to be improved, supporting the broader objective of behavior modification and allowing them to think critically about their actions, and specifically how such actions (whether positive or negative going forward) affect themselves and other people.

Hello 64758! Thank you for your well thought out reply! I'd like to take a look at this statement: "discouraging undesirable behavior through negative consequences." I don't think the consequences have to be negative. All punishment is, is discouraging a behavior, which can be done by removing or applying a stimulus. (https://pressbooks.online.ucf.edu/lumenpsychology/chapter/operant-conditioning/#:~:text=Reinforcement%20means%20you%20are%20increasing,likelihood%20of%20a%20behavioral%20response.)

Though I am of the camp that positive reinforcement works better I do think punishment does have its merits, especially if, as you say "clear expectations of acceptable behavior moving forward are conveyed through the punishment." If a learner knows what the expected behavior is, punishment does not need to be a negative experience. Discouraging a behavior need not be a negative thing. Ex: my college campus discouraged people from walking on the grass (punishment aka discouraging a behavior) by putting up signs! Nary a negative experience to be had there!

64758,

I completely agree with your last point which states, "Immediate consequences, including punishment when done in this way, can yield faster behavior modification, but it should definitely be accompanied by guidance and support to help the child understand and internalize the desired behaviors."

There is a large concern of negative effects such as fear, aggression, or lower self-esteem as a result of using punishment as a reinforcement procedure. As long as punishment is used modestly and in conjunction with reasoning for each consequence, punishment is an effective means to modifying behavior. Punishment most certainly is the quickest way for a learner to distinguish between desirable and undesirable behaviors. Driscoll refers to the works of Azrin and Holz (1996) by mentioning, "when used sparingly, punishment has the advantage of conveying information about what behaviors are considered appropriate or inappropriate in given situations" (2004, pp. 42). She also refers to Walters & Grusec (1997) when stating, ".. some behaviorists also recommend a warning precede punishment and reasons accompany it to explain why certain behaviors are not tolerated (Driscoll, 2004, pp.42). If punishment is accompanied with patience, reasoning, and virtue, it will cease the possibility of leading to more unfortunate side effects.

_(For my below writing, the term teacher describes teacher, parent, trainer, and management. The term student describes student, child, trainee, and employee.) _

Punishment (positive or negative) may work in the short term, but it lacks the building blocks for long-term behavior change. Positive reinforcement builds connections and rewards the student for modeling the desired behavior. It is the perfect recipe for long-term change.

When using positive reinforcement, the teacher is motivated by being able to reward a learner’s behavior, and the learner is motivated by feeling good about being rewarded. A confident learner who feels good about themselves is likelier to repeat the behavior. Punishment must be done soon after the undesired event and must be done consistently. The fatigue on the teacher to enforce punishment (positive or negative) can be exhausting. The interaction lacks the same positive association, and the connection runs the risk of not forming.  

The message is clear when a teacher rewards the learner for a behavior. The learner knows the behavior the teacher desires. The student has modeled the desired expectation. Punishment (negative or positive) is not as black and white. Not all punishment is severe, but when it is, it can have consequences that reach far beyond behavioral modifications. According to (DRISCOLL et al., 2022), “When punishment involves a particularly aversive stimulus or induces pain, it can lead to undesirable emotional responses being conditioned” (pg. 41). Punishment can serve as a model for aggression (DRISCOLL et al., 2022).

Hey 50400,
I agree with your overall argument that punishment lacks building blocks for long term behavior change. When I was doing my own research, I found that it can negatively impact a student's sense of self worth and self-confidence in decision making. I believe that this all makes sense because as you said, a confident learner needs to build positive relationships with their teachers in order to get the most out of their education.

While you make some good points about longer term behavior, punishment is more effective when the needs of the situation are urgent and benahiors need corrected immediately. For example, students jumping down the stairwells need to be stopped immediately so they do not injure themeselves or others. It only takes once for something horrific to happen. Positive reinforcement would require a great deal of time reinforcing the replacement benahior, while a punishment would make an immediate impact and change banavior.

Hi 60407!
I like your example because it is real life, but it did make me think. You are right; the children should be stopped. But in this scenario, no punishment should be applied (negative or positive), and positive reinforcement can be used the next time the child is not jumping down the steps.

Hi 50400! I think you overall offered an insightful argument and raised important considerations regarding positive reinforcement and its long-term impact on behavior change. Positive reinforcement can, in some instances, offer a powerful mechanism to build connections and encourage learners to model desired behavior, fostering a positive and confident learning environment. If done consistently, I think the rewards associated with positive reinforcement could create a positive association, reinforcing the behavior and encouraging its repetition. However, I think we also need to acknowledge that punishment, when applied judiciously, with clear communication, positive guidance, and explicit expectations, can also play a crucial role in behavior modification. While punishment may not always be the primary approach or necessarily the right primary approach for each child, it can still act as a positive deterrent and provide immediate consequences for undesirable behavior. But the key here is to ensure that the punishment is proportionate to the bad behavior, is fair overall, and aims to correct the behavior and promote critical thinking, rather than induce fear or anxiety.

Hi 50400,
The point you made that "the fatigue on the teacher to enforce punishment (positive or negative) can be exhausting" stood out to me because it was something I had not considered. When teachers are constantly having to give students punishments, it causes emotional turmoil for both parties involved. Driscoll (2005) stated that “…punishment is _the presentation of an aversive stimulus contingent upon a response that reduces the rate of that response” _(p. 40)._ _When people use punishment as a reinforcement, they are able to reduce someone’s bad behavior. For example, when students at my school are caught skipping class, the punishment they receive is a phone call home and in school suspension. Students avoid the punishment by not skipping class.

In addition to stopping bad behavior, punishment as a reinforcement also has the ability to prevent potentially dangerous behavior. For example, Driscoll (2005) stated that “… if a child is about to injure herself by picking up a hot iron, a fast slap on the wrist or a loud ‘NO!’ may be the most effective way to gain her attention and stop her in the act” (p. 42). In this example, the child received the punishment as a way to stop dangerous behavior before they were injured.__

            Another reason punishment is more effective than positive reinforcement is because it can be used to teach people which actions and behaviors are inappropriate. Driscoll (2005) referenced work from Azrin & Holz (1966) and Walters & Grusec (1977) when she stated that “… punishment has the advantage of conveying information about what behaviors are considered appropriate or inappropriate in given situations” (p. 42). This applies to schools because there are certain behaviors that are not appropriate for school, and having a punishment response can reduce the behavior. For example, I once had a student get mad and flip a desk. His punishment was going to the principal, and as a result of the punishment he never engaged in that behavior again. The punishments showed the student that their behavior was inappropriate for school and needed to change.

            Positive reinforcement is defined by Driscoll (2005) as “…_the presentation of a reinforcer (satisfying stimulus) contingent upon a response that results in the strengthening of that response” _(p. 37).  It does not modify bad or dangerous behavior, or teach which actions are inappropriate in different settings because positive reinforcement is meant to continue encouraging good behavior, rather the stop bad behavior. Driscoll (2005) stated that “…behavior is more likely to reoccur if it has been rewarded or reinforced” (p. 35). Therefore, if we want to end bad behavior then we must use punishment as a reinforcement, and save positive reinforcement to encourage the continuation of good behavior. In an article about positive reinforcement in the work place, Wei and Yazdanifard (2014) stated that “Positive reinforcement is highly effective in strengthening and increasing behaviors” (p. 10). For example, if a child is about to engage in dangerous behavior, such as touching an open flame, then a punishment would be the best reinforcement option at that moment because it is a bad behavior. However, if a child is engaging in safe behavior, such as putting on their seatbelt as soon as they get in the car, then one should use positive reinforcement to continue encouraging that good behavior. So, while positive reinforcement may be useful in some situations, it is not the best for trying to end bad, dangerous, or inappropriate actions.

            In conclusion, punishment is more effective than positive reinforcement because it can be used to end bad, dangerous, or inappropriate behavior more quickly. While positive reinforcement is better for encouraging good behavior, punishment is better for stopping bad behavior.

The debate as to whether or not “punishment is more effective than positive reinforcement as a method for changing behavior” is a compelling one, with strong arguments on both the “support” and “opposing” sides. After evaluating the arguments, my stance is neutral as I believe that both are effective methods in changing behavior when they are applied hand-in-hand. There is not a one-size-fits-all solution to changing behavior, and multiple methods creates an effective and more balanced approach. Since there are limitations to both approaches, a combination would prevent these limitations from shining through. For example, punishment only teaches someone what behavior not to do. It does not teach someone what behavior they should be exhibiting instead. On the other hand, positive reinforcement lets someone know that they are exhibiting the correct behavior. If a combination of the two were to be implemented, it would encourage the desired behavior and discourage the undesired behavior. For example, in a classroom setting the teacher wants their students to follow the classroom rules. Students who do this throughout the entire day will receive a free homework pass, and students not following the rules will receive extra homework to complete. The students exhibiting the desired behavior are rewarded with something enjoyable while the others are not. In turn, the students who did not follow the rules will strive to make those behavioral changes so they will receive a free homework pass as well. Both sides made very strong cases as to why either punishment or positive reinforcement was more effective for behavior change. The strongest arguments made were the ones that provided examples and cited sources from where they were getting their information. This built credibility in their argument. For example, 31035   challenged 64758 Rush’s definition of the term “consequence.” 31035 stated their argument, along with a citation to a credible source backing up their claim. In addition, 64758 Rush’s arguments stood out to me because they refuted any comment on their post for those that disagreed with them. 64758 responded with a highly detailed explanation along with valuable sources and examples. My main takeaway from the “support” side of the argument is that punishment is a quick way to immediately eradicate an undesired behavior. One will create an association between the punishment and behavior, thus lessening the likelihood of it occurring again. My main takeaway from the “oppose” side is that positive reinforcement motivates someone to do the desired behavior so they can be rewarded. This approach is lighthearted and does not have negative consequences on one’s feelings. Based on the arguments made, I feel that the “oppose” side made stronger arguments. One observation I made was that the “support” side only made arguments as to why punishment was better, with only 64758 Rush mentioning one negative impact of positive reinforcement. On the other hand, the “oppose” side made various arguments as to why punishment was bad and positive reinforcement was good. By the end of the debate, I came to my conclusion that I was neutral on the idea that punishment is more effective than positive reinforcement. Both sides made valid arguments that I found myself agreeing with. I think that these two methods collaborate well with one another and create a balance in changing behavior. The technique I used to come to this conclusion was thinking about how I might go about a situation to change a behavior. From personal experience working in a classroom setting, I use both and I find both to be equally as effective when applied in the appropriate situation.

This can help individuals to learn that certain behaviors are unacceptable and will result in negative consequences. It can also be used to deter dangerous behaviors as well as teach children about right and wrong. For example, if a child hits another child, a parent may punish the child to teach them that hitting is wrong. The proponents of this debate argued that punishment may be more effective for certain types of behavior. Punishment, for example, may be more effective for dangerous or harmful behaviors, whereas positive reinforcement may be more effective for desirable but non-emergency behaviors. Punishment can be used to establish clear limits and expectations. People are more likely to change their behavior when they are aware of which behaviors are seriously unacceptable. Arguments include that when it comes to risky behaviors, punishment is more effective than positive reinforcement; opponents argue that positive reinforcement is more effective than punishment in the long term, and punishment can have serious health consequences. The most powerful argument advanced by the support side is that when danger is imminent, punishment is effective in the face of short-term behavior; the most powerful argument advanced by the opposition side is that the guidance and role model of positive behavior is long-term, so positive reinforcement is more effective in terms of effectiveness. I am neutral on the position in this debate. I believe that both punishment and positive reinforcement have significant effects in education. For different situations, different reinforcement methods are used. To determine which strategy is more effective for behavior, evaluate the situation and characteristics of learners at the time; the condition for positive reinforcement to work is that people expect to be rewarded and place a high value on rewards (Dr. Driscoll, p65); punishment is used in emergency or short-term behaviors. Long-term punishment strategies, however, cause psychological and physical harm to learners. A long history of punishment can be physically or psychologically damaging. The phenomenon of learned helplessness may occur, especially when aversive stimuli cannot be avoided or avoided. (Dr. Driscoll, p41).

Is studying the biological and neural processes of the brain the best way to understand how people learn? Arguably, it is one beneficial way to research how to optimize academics and training; it is not the only productive way to assist students and workers in the acclimation and acquisition of information. Learning is a complex subject that is more easily understood by studying observable behavior. It is a weak critique to suggest that internal processes are unnecessary to address because it is not visually recognized. In the 21st century, we have MRI Scans and Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) to establish how the brain processes look and operate independently from outside interference. However, it is helpful to research the internal context that underlines or constructs these actions. The brain is a physical organ with biological capabilities that help us function efficiently as a species. But does everyone's body operate at the same capacity and present all the potential abilities? Cognitivism is the epistemology that aims to discover how the brain stores, processes and responds to data. Natural processes like maturation play a role in understanding what is appropriate to teach someone. Behaviorism is a learning theory that explores how behavior alters by interacting with the environment. Vygotsky suggests that learning is often socially influenced, and a skilled adult can help learners advance beyond their biologically influenced limits within the developmental process (for example, teaching critical thinking to concrete-operational children who are not naturally capable of abstract thinking). Some arguments against cognitivism are that exclusively considering the internal process determines how we learn and isolates people who are neurally divergent or raised in an environment where they did not receive the necessary love and guidance from their parents to reach their full potential academically or socially. If a student or adult trainee has a fixed mindset about themselves, the basis for this low opinion of themselves usually is not intrinsically based; their environment and interactions within it likely led them to these negative conclusions of their cognitive abilities. A defense of cognitivism is that this approach to teaching and training focuses on the process and less on the outcome. The teacher facilitates the learning and guides the learner to direct their instruction. Contrarily, behaviorism puts its ownness on the instructor to tell people what behaviors are acceptable and unacceptable based on reinforcements and punishments. If the teacher believes that her students should be quiet and listen, she might punish those who seek to share their opinions and perspectives and reward those who suppress their contrary views and those entirely subject to their approval. Understanding a person engaged in the learning process at school or work entails addressing their biological capacities and constraints without completely overlooking the necessity of influence, such as scaffolding or a more experienced role model committed to improving a learner's outcome.

In the debate discussion, the support sides identified that the internal process within the mind is crucial to understanding how learning takes place. By understanding the internal processes involved in learning, instructors can develop more effective teaching strategies and interventions that can help individuals learn more efficiently and effectively. The support sides give a lot of examples to support the statement. For example, two people might have the same positive reinforcement placed on them while they matter the same punishment even to know but they might still react differently. So, it’s important to focus on the internal processes and why this difference in learning happened. Another example, an elementary teacher is confused and suffered by a student’s behavior performance, the poor student can’t try to listen to the teacher at the same time he is attracted by other classmates’ behaviors. After knowing his age and learning level, and then understanding the learner’s working memory capacity, attentional process, and his ability to control attention in both a general and specific sense, appears to differ with age, and the ability to transfer knowledge from one context to another, the teacher recognized that the student’s short-term memory takes longer time to react and rehearsal. After understanding the internal process, the teacher could arrange and provide specific instruction to enhance learners’ encoding and memory. On the opposing sides, while understanding the internal processes within the mind is certainly important for effective learning, it is not the only factor that determines successful instruction. They argued that internal mental processes are not directly observable and therefore cannot be studied scientifically, and all behavior is shaped by the environment through conditioning, including an automatic response is elicited by a previously neutral stimulus such as hungry, or through operant conditioning, where behavior is strengthened or weakened based on its consequences such as positive reinforcement and punishment. At the same time, they emphasized the importance of the environment because it creates a safe and encouraging space for individuals to learn. The role of external factors such as social environment, cultural context, and educational resources play very essentially in shaping how individuals learn. One of arguments to refute the statement is the Nine Steps of Gagne’s “Event of Instruction”. For instance, Gagne's model emphasizes the importance of providing clear objectives, presenting information in a meaningful way, and providing opportunities for learners to practice and receive feedback. These steps are focused on external factors such as the design of instruction and the quality of feedback provided, rather than solely on internal processes within the mind. In my opinion, a comprehensive understanding of learning should include an examination of both internal processes and external behaviors. While internal processes within the mind play a crucial role in learning, external factors such as the design of instruction, feedback provided, and opportunities for practice and application are equally important.  As educators, we should adjust teaching strategies and learning theories that are suitable for the target audiences to achieve learning outcomes. For instance, to explain declarative and procedural knowledge in an instructor’s classroom, considering the complex and abstract concept, the instructor can provide organized instruction to increase the long interest of individuals. These instructional tactics are reflected on the stages and processes of cognitive information processing. To enhance encoding and retrieval, graphic representations have been particularly effective in facilitating memory storage of information, such as concept maps, if designed well, they should assist the instructors in organizing and understanding the concepts discussed. But the event that we talked about in the debate, about trying to teach someone a motor skill such as riding a bike, can we use a procedural graphic to teach? Can we solve this problem only by the internal processes within the mind? Obviously not. Firstly, external behavior and environment will be the first consideration. Proving a safe environment for practice, demonstrating the practice to let the learners watch and learn, and then breaking down the task into manageable steps, and providing clear and timely feedback, these processes offer a good way to teach riding a bike.  If in a specific situation, for example, the learner has emotional learning problems, such as difficulty and complexity to influence attention, we educators should teach the learner to take more time in responding to a learning task, and in a strategy way for focusing attention and allow to practice that strategy. ( Dr. Driscoll, p80)

Cognativeismt helps grab students’ attention because you can tailor student experiences to their specific learning processes.Keeping in mind the prioritization of knowledge (it takes time to store information,) as well as levels of what should be taught allow students to succeed. We need to know when and where to teach, and how much depending on the age of the student. Behavior/relationships can be more important the internal processes when it comes to learning (AKA; they can almost overcome internal learning) Helps grab students’ attention because you can tailor student experiences to their specific learning needs A lot of times cognitivism just isn’t practical–you can teach without knowing the processes of the brain. As a member of the opposing team, I argued that educators provide students with the intro/basics for understanding new material. Teachers introduce students to concepts, theories, and principles, which open the door for learning. Without this support, learners may not be able to engage in the material on their own. Members supporting the statement argued against this opposing thought saying that, “without active engagement and constructed knowledge from the learner, the information presented by the teacher is useless”. Members of the supporting team mentioned the learners are ultimately in charge of constructing their own knowledge and that the teacher is merely a facilitator. While their point was clear, it was argued that in order for a constructivist learning environment to be successful, the teacher is the only one that can construct activities that are meant to educate the learner. Furthermore, some learners are in need of support in constructing their own  that only a teacher can provide. After engaging in the debate, I realized the original statement holds truth but it also limits the teacher to a particular type of ‘instruction’. I think the transmission of information for classrooms functioning in the constructivist method occurs when teachers create activities that are meant to teach students in a way where they are held accountable for understanding certain information.

The debate on whether “knowledge cannot be instructed (transmitted) by a teacher, only constructed by the learner” came with strong arguments presented from both the supporting and opposing sides. The key takeaway from the supporting side of the debate is that students must actively take initiative in their learning process in order for knowledge to be constructed. The teacher is there to lead them with the appropriate resources, but it is the student’s responsibility to process the information. Their argument reminds me of the phrase “you can lead a horse to water, but you can't make it drink.” This signifies that teachers can provide learners with all the necessary resources and activities to understand the materials, but learners need to make sense of the content to construct it. There are three distinct arguments made by the supporting side. This includes the notion that teachers only passively transmit knowledge through lecture and students must make sense of it themselves. Teachers are simply facilitators in the learning process. Hands-on experiences allow students to make connections and the teacher is there to be of assistance if needed. The strongest argument made on this team was by 42489. Their frequent citing of various sources in the textbook strengthened their argument. Providing the textbook reference pages served as supplemental material in support of their argument. After re-reading those pages, I found myself agreeing with their argument because it was supported by evidence. The key takeaway from the opposing side of the debate is that teachers play the critical role as a facilitator in the learning process. Teachers have been educated on and trained to instruct content in the best way for students based on their learning needs and prerequisite knowledge. Teachers design and deliver lessons and activities based on these components. With their guidance, learners can effectively construct knowledge because they are placed in a learning environment that facilitates this process. There is one distinct argument made by this side. This includes that teachers know the learning needs of students and take those into account when lesson planning. They know what types of questions to ask, what material to incorporate, and how to guide students in achieving their goals. The strongest argument made on this side was by 31035. Before presenting their arguments, they included definitions of terms that were significant in the post. This sets the stage for a strong argument. I appreciate their two ways of looking at the debate, through an “absolute” and a “practicality” lens. Based on the arguments made, it is evident that the learning process is complex. To say that “knowledge can only be constructed by the learner” has many limitations. In order for a learning environment to be effective, the teacher and student must have the willingness to participate. My final stance on the statement “knowledge cannot be instructed (transmitted) by a teacher, only constructed by the learner” is that I agree with the opposing side. While I do agree that knowledge must be constructed by the learner, teachers also play a critical role in this process. I came to this conclusion by considering how students learn in the Pre-K class I teach. I facilitate their learning process by asking them questions and providing them with the necessary materials to transfer knowledge. If this facilitation were not present, it would be more difficult for them to make connections, therefore, I feel that knowledge is instructed (transmitted) by both teacher and learner, not by the learner only.

Knowledge cannot be instructed (transmitted) by a teacher, only constructed by the learner. This week’s debate was both the easiest and most difficult for me. Firstly, the prompt I was asked to support was very close to my belief set about education, as I’ve largely used a constructivist approach to teaching for most of my career. So, finding examples and leaning on my own pedagogical stance helped form my central arguments for this week. But, this technology platform was the most difficult for me to use and, in my opinion, one of the hardest in which to develop a full discussion of points in an argument. Perhaps because I am new to this platform, or because I am an “geriatric millennial” “x-ennial,” the discourse here felt disjointed and as though people made the same arguments over and over again without advancing new ideas. As per Driscol and the video from this week, constructivism is premised on the idea that teachers do not convey all learning to students, but rather function as a facilitator, guiding students to learn and explore.  My background is that of an ELA and social studies teacher, and in my work I’ve guided students to explore materials that are impactful to them and have supported students when and where they struggle. Through inquiry and project based learning, students in my classes have an opportunity to deeply examine ideas and create products to reflect the learning they do during the course of a unit. While I assist them with certain aspects of the learning, I often learn alongside them as their questions sometimes move into areas where I might not have full expertise. My job as the instructor is to design the learning experience so students develop the skills, knowledge, and habits along the way as they find things they are curious about in the content we are learning. I felt as though few people clearly understood that constructivism isn’t simply leaving students alone to their own devices. Rather, it is a partnership between teacher and students to learn together and dig into material in order to give students space and ability to understand the knowledge they need to gain. I truly believe the most lasting knowledge is gained through these methods, as doing makes the knowledge more “sticky” for the learner. I will admit that I think it would be hard for any teacher to be a fully constructivist instructor who never uses cognitivism or behaviorism as part of their instructional plan. When fully immersed in PBL and inquiry learning work, I am probably around 80% constructivist, as there are times it is important to simply lay out guidelines or understandings. However, that learning is the least likely to stick in my experience, unless students then use it to make sense of the ideas they are learning and using in their work.

For example, a classmate on the supporting side brought up the connection between apprenticeships and constructivism. Of course, as in any absolute statement, there will be debate regarding its validity or inaccuracy. The position of our class discussion states, "Knowledge cannot be instructed (transmitted) by a teacher, only constructed by the learner." This assertion relates to constructivism, which is the epistemology that emphasizes the student as the director of their learning with the limited interference and intervention of the instructor. Knowledge does not develop only because of the teacher or student; it must be a collective effort. I noticed that the team who offered refutation to the opening position adhered to behaviorism, which reflects the traditional approach to the classroom environment where the teacher designs lesson plans and disciplines the pupils; students passively follow the classroom rules and expectations. An argument against constructivism is that subjects that require extensive training should involve direct instruction from a skilled and experienced individual. Imagine if surgeons or architects only used YouTube videos and online courses in medical school. Having people train themselves in highly skilled disciplines would be a nightmare for their customer base. Another potential issue with constructivism is that students need careful guidance to become critical and reflective learners. If teachers take too much of a hands-off approach in the classroom, the students will not receive a strong enough foundation of skill sets and strategies they can use in future classroom activities and assignments. However, student-centered learning can create lessons that are more inclusive and reflective of the needs of the individual learners. Driscoll (2005) states that constructivism is the process by which students adopt and adapt new information to add to previously learned topics. Collaborative instruction allows peers to teach and challenge others about what they know and are attempting to learn. According to an American Physicist, Frank Oppenheimer, " the best way to learn is to teach." It is essential to give students opportunities to apply their learnings in projects and team projects to acquire a realistic perspective of how the knowledge applies to reality. However, the teacher should engage in direct instruction to model and provide clarifying details to help students categorize and organize knowledge effectively.

In doing so, they facilitate learning. An effective approach to teaching is to provide students with opportunities to actively construct their own knowledge. This can be done through hands-on activities, problem-solving, and collaborative learning experiences. In these settings, students are encouraged to think critically, ask questions, and share their ideas with others. As students engage in these activities, they are able to build their own understanding of the concepts being taught. In conclusion, I believe that when students are actively engaged in the learning process and constructing their own knowledge, they are more likely to learn and retain the information. Additionally, they are better able to apply their knowledge to new situations.

After carefully reviewing all of the arguments presented on both sides of the debate, my final position and viewpoints on the debated claim agree with that statement. The supporting argument and examples are numerous, and the opposing argument and examples are weak. I support that knowledge can only be constructed by the learner, not be constructed, or transmitted by a teacher. Learning is a social activity; every student's interaction with others is essential for knowledge construction; they begin the learning journey with some prior knowledge and then build their understanding on top of that. For example, medical students rely on heuristics rather than well-formed rules to successfully diagnose a medical problem (p395). Heuristics refers to students actively participating in determining their own learning needs and how those needs can be best met to solve the real and unique medical symptoms they encounter. Instructors discovered that when medical students rely too heavily on "direct instruction" from a teacher or oversimplify general theories, they disregard unique or puzzling symptoms and make diagnostic errors. As a result, instructors take on the role of facilitator rather than director, and students construct and reconstruct their own knowledge. One argument from the opposing side is that teachers play a critical role in the learning process by introducing students to concepts, theories, and principles. While this is true, it's important to note that it's only the first step in the learning process. Without active engagement and constructed knowledge from the learner, the information presented by the teacher is useless. In our current debate discussion, for example, the professor's creation of a complex, realistic, and social environment has allowed us to delve deeply into the question of constructivism's validity. We are now actively thinking, drawing on our individual past experiences, and listening to other classmates' perspectives to construct and reconstruct our understanding of the knowledge presented in the textbook. The opposing side also argues that special education learners may have difficulty learning by themselves and need extra one-on-one help to construct knowledge. However, constructivism creates a social environment that is realistic and relevant, providing a good chance for special needs learners to connect with the real world. In this educational environment, they can learn from examples and learn by doing, enabling them to achieve deep levels of understanding and construct knowledge themselves. While the teacher-centered approach is more effective than the student-centered approach for enhancing academic achievement, only the active learner is a successful learner.

The claim being debated this week states that, “Knowledge cannot be instructed (transmitted) by a teacher, only constructed by the learner.” After analyzing the arguments from individuals on both sides of the claim, I formed my final position as neutral, neither agree or disagree with the claim. My final position to remain neutral was a result of the following criteria: the number of arguments, which arguments were backed with evidence, what side of the claim had weaker arguments, and the overall quality in each response on both sides of the claim. When reading through the Discord responses, the number of arguments posted were pretty much the same amount for both sides of the claim. Majority of the claims posted on Discord had a counter-response from someone on the opposite side of the claim. Each side posted reasonable arguments that were sound and justified. When reviewing stronger arguments provided on both sides, individuals from each side of the claim incorporated evidence from the text or from personal experiences. On the supporting side, 43179 makes strong arguments that learning is an active and continuous process. Learners have to store and process information, in addition to adapting in order to perceive the external experiences around them. She also alludes to the idea that constructivism is similar to other theories such as Piaget’s Developmental Model or Vygotsky’s & Bruner’s idea of reconstruction of knowledge. 49753 also provides evidence from Driscoll which mentions that “knowledge is constructed by learners as they attempt to make sense of their experiences” (2004, pp. 387). There were also a couple arguments that were backed by evidence on the opposing side. 31035 provided definitions for behaviorism, cognitivism and constructivism, and proceeded to oppose the claim because of absolutes and practicality. 5259 provides examples of ways that teachers actually transmit knowledge to learners using various instructional tools and strategies. Each side presented strong arguments to advocate for their side of the claim. The opposing side did provide some weaker arguments regarding some examples and also primarily focusing on the terminology of the claim. 50400 opposed the claim by using examples regarding richer application and societal norms such as teachers addressing students who “run in the hallway or parents of adopted children learned from adopted grown-ups how to be better parents.” I provided a counter-argument that suggested that students still have to form the construct on their own of why it is not reasonable to run in the hallway. Addressing the other example, a child who was raised without parents or in a struggling home and later adopted, has an innate desire to be better like those parents who adopted them for their own offspring. Therefore, creating a sense of self-regulation and willingness to learn. In addition to the weaker examples opposing the claim, some individuals specifically targeted the word “only” suggesting that people do not only learn through constructing their own knowledge and experiences. Majority of the arguments presented on either side of the claim were reasonable, justified, and valid. I decided to take a neutral stance on this claim because the supporting side provided substantial evidence supporting the theory that knowledge is constructed by the learner. Whereas, the opposing side had sound reasoning as to how teachers transmit knowledge and instruct learners on how to achieve specific learning targets.

Again, I think that support team had more supporting points. This is a common theme from all three debates.

As far as this debate’s content goes, I personally agree and disagree with the statement, though my assigned position was to support.
