For Module 6’s debate, the statement for discussion was “Knowledge cannot be instructed (transmitted) by a teacher, only constructed by the learner”, a common position held by many constructivist theorists. One of the arguments for supporting the statement was that learning is a social activity and also that everyone’s learning journey begins with some prior knowledge that is expanded/built upon as we generate new experiences. Also, information can be presented by an instructor but it is still up to the learner to make use of the information presented. As an example of the supporting side of the debate, one participant noted that the debate was an example of knowledge construction by the learner. Another argument made for supporting statements was that young children/infants who are not in school still learn/construct knowledge even though they may not have a ‘teacher’ (school/formal teacher besides parents). One argument made opposing the statement was that educators sometimes provide the introduction of some new concepts to students and thus initiate learners being able to learn content. Another argument made by the opposing side was that instructors can provide access to a wide variety of resources which would help to “enrich” the learning experience and also help the process of students making connections with experiences and prior knowledge. Teachers can also help with seeing where students may have not fully grasped a concept (for example with a math course).

My final position on the debated claim "Knowledge cannot be instructed (transmitted) by a teacher, only constructed by the learner" is that I strongly disagree with this statement. I think a lot of the knowledge I have has been transmitted by teachers. I think that our school systems are set up the way they are because teachers guide students towards learning certain information that they may not come across otherwise. I think formal education is extremely important. I do think that knowledge can be instructed by the learner but the statement says knowledge can only be constructed by the learner. I think the opposing side presented more arguments to support their position. We gave different examples of how teachers transmit knowledge. I think the opposing side gave good examples for how learners construct knowledge, but not enough about how teachers don't transmit knowledge. I felt like they weren't arguing for how knowledge can only be constructed by the learner. The strongest argument presented on the supporting side would be "Each individual has their own set of prior experiences and prior knowledge on things. Based upon new experiences, students will begin to construct new knowledge and incorporate the new experiences into their knowledge." The strongest argument from the opposing side would be, "I oppose the statement and want to argue that educators provide students with the intro/basics for understanding new material. They introduce students to concepts, theories, and principles, which open the door for learning. Without this support, learners may not be able to engage in the material on their own." I believe that both learners and teachers can construct/transmit knowledge, and it is not only the learners that can do so.

Another great opportunity to learn from my peers! I’ve gathered a good sample of the arguments made by each side, but will summarize them below as well. Supporting: Knowledge is actively constructed by a learner, built on previous background knowledge. This differs from what a teacher usually does: passively transmit knowledge via lecture. Passive learning does not allow students to actively make connections between information. Information sticks better if the information is taught in context- specific environment. Encourages practicing the behavior/what is learned. Teacher’s role should be to facilitate: Integrate learning experiences with their existing understanding of the world. Apply experiences that are related to students’ prior experiences. Meaningful learning is rarely solidified by simply listening to another person lecture. Apprenticeship models are a thing. Experiences are the impetus that gives knowledge directly to the learner. Opposing: Teachers have a role: When the topic is not easily learner-driven (ex: maths). To explain why something is beneficial. To organize the opportunity to learn and set up good environments for learning. Share basic information that students would waste their time learning otherwise or to quickly correct student misunderstandings. Developing a student/teacher relationship to increase buy-in. To provide structure. Hard to take full ownership of learning, especially when students do not have the self-sufficiency to do so. Creating “complete and relevant” environments is hard and expensive to do. If knowledge cannot be instructed/transmitted, why are children sent to preschools, etc? Constructivism is already very closely tied to the other theories we have learned about. It is impossible to break them apart. Most supporting arguments stressed the importance of constructivism’s innate and inbuilt active learning, as well as the helpfulness of learning within the context of the problems the students will have to solve. They also corrected misunderstandings about the role of an instructor within constructivist experience: learning might not be transmitted by the instructor, but the instructor does have a place in learning. They are there to create the correct environment for learners, as well as support and encourage them to reflect and ask questions. Most opposing arguments stressed the importance of the instructor for roles that they might not be able to hold in a constructivist learning environment. Arguments also talked about the difficulty of asking students to take full ownership of their learning, especially when they don’t have the self-sufficiency to do so. Arguments also talked about the difficulty (and thus impracticality) of creating the “complete and relevant” environments constructivist theories require. One argument I will make against constructivism within a formal education setting is that I don’t think it is often done right. I’ll be using my high school chemistry class for a couple of examples. In this class, we used lots of learner experiences to teach us principles. I remember the activities (making ice cream, boiling eggs, etc) but I don’t remember what principles it was supposed to teach me. The same thing happened in the two chemistry classes I had to take in college. I attended the lectures, and learned the material. Then, I had to waste several hours of my busy week going to a lab that did nothing to reinforce the learning that I had already done. I still think there is a place for instructors, especially if the instructor holds space for students to ask questions that arise. This one of the roles an instructor plays in constructivism. I don’t see any harm in explaining to students why they are learning something, and what the learning should teach them. Instructors can then allow the constructivist activity afterwards to help students apply the learning in a way that sticks with them. For example of where this concept could have helped: my high school chemistry class. We had to complete an activity, without a lecture, in order to learn a principle. I never learned the principle, and the instructor never covered the information in class. I did the experiment (incorrectly, I might add, but had no concept of the “correct way” to do the experiment) and to this day, I don’t know what I was supposed to have learned from it. In this regard, the constructivist theory failed my learning, and it could have been saved by the power of an instructor. All that complaining aside, I actually do love the concept of Constructivism, done right. At the end of the debate, I still feel much the same as I did at the beginning: constructivism is already so closely tied to other learning theories that it would be impossible to have constructivism without the other learning theories. BUT, I do think there is a great place for constructivist theories in the world. I love the buy-in that comes when students construct their own learning and models of the world. This is a design practice that I use frequently in my own consultations: allowing student choice creates more buy-in all around.

As we've been learning in this class thus far, within constructivist theories of learning, knowledge is essentially viewed as actively constructed by the learner, built upon their previous background knowledge, experiences, and/or skills. Acquiring knowledge is an active, ongoing process that allows the individual to promote meaningful, growing understanding of complex concepts. This differs from what a teacher is typically meant to do, as they passively transmit knowledge and information, often in a lecture-based technique. Doing so does not always allow the learner to actively make connections between information, or actively engage with active recall of previously acquired knowledge. The statement, ‚"knowledge cannot be instructed by a teacher, only constructed by the learner,‚" thus argues that learners must actively engage with new information and experiences, integrating them within their existing understanding of the world to create new knowledge. When a learner interacts with information, interprets it, and applies it to solve problems or make sense of the world for example, true understanding and knowledge is then cultivated. The role of the teacher can facilitate this process by providing guidance and opportunities for exploration, however, it's up to the learner to then interpret, critically think about, and apply that knowledge alongside everything they've learned in their lives thus far. Therefore, in line with constructivist theories, it can be argued that knowledge is indeed constructed by the learner through their active involvement in the learning process.

First, some definitions and groundwork (And please correct me if I'm wrong!)
**Behaviorism **is concerned with the external proof of learning, rather than the internal processes. Uses behaviors to prove that learning has happened, and ‚"teaching‚" is done through positive- or negative- reinforcement or punishment. Behaviorism is objectivist, which holds the opinion that a learner is an empty vessel which can be filled.

**Cognitivism **was developed in response to behaviorism and is concerned with the internal processes of learning‚Äìthe ‚"how‚" of learning. Most cognitivist thoughts can be thought of as an input, which the brain then processes, resulting in an output. While behaviorists would be more interested in the output, cognitivists care more about the inputs and the processes of the brain. Cognitivists, though, are still objectivists, which believe that the learner is an empty vessel waiting to be filled.

**Constructivism **is not objectivist. Constructivism believes that the learner plays an active role in constructing their own knowledge. I like to think of it as a learner chipping away at a block of marble, which represents the world. What they create through their learning may or may not be how the world ‚"actually is‚" but it is a good enough representation to get them through until their understanding requires them to change or scrap the model entirely.

In a way, then, this argument is between objectivism (which includes Cognitivism and Behaviorism) and non-objectivism (in this case, constructivist thinking.)Two reasons to oppose:

**Absolutes**: To say something is the ‚"only‚" way is to ignore the inherent usefulness of other ways of learning. Constructivism is very closely tied to the ideas of Cognitivism and are hard to separate. Our book mentioned Vygotsky multiple times in the chapter about constructivism, even though Vygostky's theories are considered Congativist. Vygostky's methods use a More Knowledgeable Other. Constructivists, too, hold a place for instructors, which create the learning environment necessary for students to learn. In a way, the instructor is transmitting what needs to be learned to the student.

Practicality: Constructivism isn't practical in all circumstances. If we also look at how learning happens in the here and the now, our classrooms are set up with an instructor who lectures or provides the materials for students to learn. Even if there is no instructor in a course, the students will read through books, which serve as their instructor. For lower level learning environments, it makes sense to have someone there, sharing the information, so that students can spend time critically thinking, rather than reinventing the wheel. This actually leaves more time for the reflexivity that constructivists enjoy so much!

Hi 50400!  I am on the supporting side and I wanted to explore your statement regarding the societal norm examples you mentioned. You provide the examples of a child running in the hallway and individuals learning how to be better parents from adopted grown-ups. With the running in the hallway example, I see where the teacher "instructs" or demands the student to stop running; however, the student will not fully understand the reasoning behind the demand provided by the teacher until he makes the connection of why he should stop running. From a constructivist standpoint, learning takes place when that student can form the concept that running in the hallway results in hurting oneself or another. The example of adopted children learning to become better parents for their own children is an excellent example related to constructivism. The adopted individuals have a desire and need to learn. A child who was raised without parents or in a struggling home and later adopted, has an innate desire to be better like those parents who adopted them for their own offspring, therefore creating a sense of self-regulation and willingness to learn.

Your notion of students needing guidance still supports a constructivist view of learning. Students build knowledge with a "guide" as instructor, very much like preschool teachers do day in and day out.  These teachers nurture the love of learning through experiences and play to gain skills, not through lectures or repetition in the same old way.

I'm not sure how the mentor as guide supports anything except constructivism. As Driscoll and the video from this week both stated, constructivist teachers aren't absent, but are guides who allow students to lead much of the learning and who support as students encounter difficulties. This is definitely much like the apprenticeship model my father used with inexperienced technicians when training them as mechanics.
